lead: A force does two jobs on a rigid body: it pushes the body along a line, and it twists the body about a point or an axis. The moment measures that twist. It explains why a long spanner loosens a rusted bolt, why a door handle sits far from the hinge, and why a crane can tip when a load swings. This chapter builds the scalar rule M = F d, the vector rule M_O = r × F, and the axis rule M_AB = u · (r × F).
prereq: You need Unit 1 vector algebra and the cross product, plus 2.1 for the line of action.

blocks.text: Fix a point O on a body. Call O the moment centre. A force F acts at some point A. The moment of F about O measures how strongly F tries to rotate the body about O. The size is M = F d. Here F is the force in newtons (N), d is the perpendicular distance in metres (m) from O to the line of action of F, and M is the moment in newton metres (N·m).

The distance d is not the distance OA. It is the shortest distance from O to the line along which F acts. A force aimed straight at O has d = 0 and gives no moment about O. A force at the same distance but more perpendicular gives a larger moment.

In a plane, use a sign: anticlockwise is positive, clockwise is negative. In space, use the right-hand rule: curl the fingers from r to F, and the thumb points along M_O. The moment changes if you choose a different point O, because both d and the direction of turning can change.
Sliding F along its line of action does not change M about a fixed O. That is the principle of transmissibility in action. It lets you pick a convenient point on the line when you compute r.

Draw a position vector r from O to any point on the line of action of F. The vector moment is M_O = r × F. This single cross product carries both the size and the axis of the turning effect. Its direction is perpendicular to both r and F, as the right-hand rule gives.
The size checks out. The cross product has magnitude r F sinθ, where θ is the angle between r and F. The perpendicular distance is d = r sinθ. So |M_O| = F d, the same scalar rule as before.
M_O = r × F = (yF_z − zF_y)i + (zF_x − xF_z)j + (xF_y − yF_x)k
blocks.where: r = x i + y j + z k is the position vector from O to the force point, in m; F = F_x i + F_y j + F_z k is the force, in N; M_O is the moment vector, in N·m.

blocks.text: Order matters. r × F and F × r have opposite signs. Take r from the moment point to the point where the force acts. A common exam slip is to reverse the order and lose the sign.

A door has a hinge axis. A push on the door may have a large moment about a point on the hinge, but only the part along the hinge actually turns the door. The moment about an axis is the component of M_O along that axis.
Let the axis pass through points A and B. Define the unit vector u = (B − A)/|B − A|. Unit means |u| = 1. Pick r from any point on the axis to the point of application of F. Then M_AB = u · (r × F).
M_AB = u · (r × F) = u_x(yF_z − zF_y) + u_y(zF_x − xF_z) + u_z(xF_y − yF_x)
blocks.where: u = u_x i + u_y j + u_z k is the unit vector along the axis AB; r = x i + y j + z k runs from any point on the axis to the force point, in m; F is the force in N; M_AB is the scalar moment about the axis, in N·m.

blocks.text: This is a scalar triple product. Written as a 3×3 determinant, the first row is u, the second row is r, and the third row is F. The result is a signed scalar, not a vector. Its sign gives the sense along u.

items: F is parallel to the axis: r × F is perpendicular to u, so the dot product is zero.
F cuts the axis: r and F are parallel, so r × F = 0.
The axis passes through the point of application of F: r = 0.

blocks.text: Some syllabi call this the moment of a force about a line. Check that u is a unit vector before you dot. Using a non-unit vector along the axis gives a wrong scale.

figure.caption: Point O is the moment centre, r runs to the point A where F acts, and the dashed line PQ is the axis. Notice that the axis need not pass through O or A.

spec.aria: A position vector r runs from the moment centre O to the point A where force F acts, and a separate dashed line PQ marks the axis about which the moment is taken.

examples.question: A force F = 3i + 4j − 2k N acts at the point A(1, 2, 3) m. Find its moment about the origin O, and its moment about the x-axis.
steps: Write the position vector from O to A: r = 1i + 2j + 3k m.
Use the component form of M_O = r × F. Here x = 1, y = 2, z = 3 and F_x = 3, F_y = 4, F_z = −2.
The x-axis has unit vector u = i. The moment about the x-axis is M_x itself: M_AB = u · M_O = −16 N·m.
The negative sign means 16 N·m clockwise when you look along +x.
examples.answer: M_O = −16i + 11j − 2k N·m, and the moment about the x-axis is −16 N·m, i.e. 16 N·m clockwise looking along +x.

traps: Writing F × r instead of r × F flips the sign of M_O. Take r from the moment point to the force point.
In M = F d, d is the perpendicular distance to the line of action, not the distance OA to the point of application.
Moment about an axis needs a unit vector u. A vector along the axis with length not 1 scales M_AB wrongly.
Moment has units N·m; do not drop the metre or call it N. The same unit as energy does not make moment an energy.
Moment about an axis is a scalar component. Do not report it as a vector unless the question asks for the moment vector about a point.

quiz.q: Define the moment of a force about a point, and give its SI unit.
quiz.a: The moment of a force F about a point O is the turning effect F produces about O. Its size is M = F d, where d is the perpendicular distance from O to the line of action. The SI unit is N·m.

quiz.q: Why does a force whose line of action passes through O have zero moment about O?
quiz.a: The perpendicular distance from O to the line of action is d = 0, so M = F d = 0. In vector form, r and F are parallel, so r × F = 0.

quiz.q: A force of 50 N acts at a perpendicular distance of 0.4 m from point O and tends to turn the body anticlockwise. Find the moment about O.
quiz.a: M = F d = 50 × 0.4 = 20 N·m. The sign is positive by the anticlockwise-positive convention, so M = +20 N·m.

quiz.q: A force F = 2i − 3j + 4k N acts at r = 1i + 2j − 1k m from O. Find M_O.
A nonzero force F acts on a body. Give two situations where its moment about an axis AB is zero.
quiz.a: The moment about axis AB is zero when F is parallel to AB, because r × F is perpendicular to u. It is also zero when F cuts AB, because r and F are parallel and r × F = 0. A third case is when the axis passes through the point of application of F, so r = 0.

quiz.q: A calculation gives the moment about the x-axis as −16 N·m. What does the negative sign tell you?
quiz.a: The sign follows the right-hand rule along +x. A negative value means the turning sense is opposite to the positive sense, that is, 16 N·m clockwise when looking along +x.

beyond: Not for the exam. Robotics uses the same cross product as a torque in joint controllers. Finite element software assembles nodal forces into moment vectors to check structures. Biomechanics uses moments at joints to size prosthetics. Search for moment vector, scalar triple product, and moment about an axis to see animations.
